title: A Aftermath for the Undertow
premise: Oscar Halloran, a bridge inspector who measures his marriage in expansion joints and keeps a careful inventory of everything unsaid, returns to the coastal town of Undertow for his mother's funeral. There, a stranger named Wren addresses the family by a name nobody uses — 'the Ferrows' — and produces a letter in his mother's handwriting that Oscar cannot read: a sentence written in a private family cipher she invented decades ago and never taught him. As dementia had already been erasing her memory, the letter is her last act of translation, and decoding it forces Oscar to confront the truth that his father did not die when he was told he did, that Wren is his half-brother, and that his mother chose loyalty to a lie over truth to her sons for forty years. In the end, Oscar reads the translated sentence aloud at the graveside — 'I kept you both, one in light and one in salt water' — and chooses to build something new with Wren rather than preserve the architecture of silence.
about_author: Noor Eastwick is the pen name of a former structural engineer who spent eleven years inspecting coastal bridges before turning to fiction full-time. They live in a converted pilot's cottage on the Atlantic seaboard, where they write about families the way tides write about shorelines.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On the drive to Undertow for his mother Marion's funeral, Oscar inspects a failing bridge and notes how his marriage to Priya has widened into gaps he can measure but not close. He catalogs what he never said to his mother. Emotional beat: controlled grief hiding behind professional precision.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the wake, a stranger named Wren arrives uninvited and calls the Hallorans 'the Ferrow family,' stunning Oscar's aunt Dee. Wren leaves before questions form, dropping a weathered envelope on the table. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family's polished surface.

chapters.title: Salt Water Cipher
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: chapters of Marion's 1980s diary interleaved with Oscar's present. The envelope contains a single handwritten sentence in a cipher Marion invented as a girl — one Oscar remembers seeing on her kitchen notepads all his life. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Tide Took
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren explains why he came: Marion wrote to him monthly for years, then stopped eight months ago when her dementia deepened. He shows Oscar postcards signed 'your mother.' Oscar refuses to believe it. Emotional beat: hostility between brothers who don't yet know they are brothers.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya finds Oscar's notebooks — decades of measured observations, including pages about her — and realizes he has been documenting their marriage instead of living in it. She confronts him gently. Emotional beat: the marriage's own undertow becomes visible.

chapters.title: The Ferrow House
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar and Wren break into the shuttered Ferrow house on the point, where Marion grew up, and find her childhood cipher key carved into a window frame. Aunt Dee catches them and confesses she always knew about Wren's mother. Emotional beat: loyalty to the dead mother beginning to war with truth.

chapters.title: Dee's Forty Years
chapters.summary: Aunt Dee's POV. Dee recounts the night Oscar's father learned of Marion's first love and left; how Marion buried the story so completely that even Dee helped bury it. The cipher sentence, Dee believes, was Marion's apology she could never speak aloud. Emotional beat: complicity examined, forgiveness withheld.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A storm floods Undertow; Wren nearly drowns checking on the Ferrow house, and Oscar pulls him out. In the aftermath, raw and soaked, they finally say the word 'brother' aloud. Emotional beat: crisis forcing intimacy; the found-family theme crystallizes.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, climax. Using the window-frame key and Marion's diaries, Oscar decodes the sentence through a long night while Priya sits with him, their first real conversation in years happening wordlessly beside him. The decoded line reveals everything: 'I kept you both, one in light and one in salt water.' Emotional beat: devastating clarity.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the graveside, Oscar reads the sentence aloud to the town, ending the family's long silence. He asks Wren to stay; he and Priya agree to rebuild honestly or part kindly. Final image: Oscar inspecting the old bridge one last time and passing it fit for another decade. Emotional beat: resolution — truth chosen over loyalty to the lie, and a new family load-rated to hold.
